client: I've been having a really hard time at family get-togethers lately, and honestly I'm not sure what to do about it. Ever since my grandmother passed away six months ago, being around my relatives just feels... hollow, I guess. Like everyone's trying to act normal and I'm just standing there feeling completely alone in a room full of people who are supposed to be my family. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: What you're describing — that sense of being surrounded by people yet feeling completely invisible in your grief — is such a painful and isolating experience, and I want you to know it makes a lot of sense given what you've been through. I'm also noticing that even as you share something so heavy, there's a kind of rushing quality to your words, almost like part of you is bracing for this not to matter — and I want to gently push back on that, because what you're feeling *does* matter. Losing your grandmother has clearly shifted something fundamental in how those family spaces feel to you, and that's exactly the kind of thing worth exploring together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess you're right that I was kind of rushing through it, like I was waiting for you to tell me to just move on or that everyone grieves differently or something. It's weird to hear that it actually matters, because at the family gatherings everyone just kind of... keeps going, and I start to wonder if I'm being dramatic for still feeling this way about losing her. She's been gone for eight months now and I still feel like there's this hollow space at every family event where she used to be.
therapist: The fact that you're still feeling her absence so deeply after eight months isn't dramatic — it's a sign of how meaningful she was to you, and grief doesn't follow a calendar or care what everyone else in the room is doing. I notice there's something in the way you're speaking — a kind of high-strung urgency, like you're half-expecting to be corrected — and I wonder if that voice telling you you're "being dramatic" is something you've absorbed from the atmosphere at these gatherings, rather than something that's actually true. It might be worth gently examining that thought: what would it mean about *you* if you were still grieving, versus what does it actually say about the depth of your love for her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but I also keep thinking... what if I actually am just being dramatic and I've convinced myself it's grief so I don't have to face that? Like, my aunt made a comment at Easter about how my grandmother "lived a full life" and we should be "celebrating, not mourning," and I couldn't tell if she was wrong or if I was just being selfish for still being sad. It's hard to separate what I actually feel from what I think I'm supposed to feel at this point.
therapist: That question you're asking — "what if I'm just being dramatic?" — is itself worth examining, because the fact that you're grieving doesn't mean you haven't also accepted that she lived a full life; both things can be true at the same time. I notice your voice carries a kind of strained, searching quality right now, like you're working very hard to figure out the "correct" answer, and I want to gently point out that the very effort you're putting into questioning your own grief suggests someone who is being deeply honest with themselves — not someone manufacturing feelings to avoid something. Your aunt's comment reflects *her* way of coping, but it doesn't get to define the terms of your loss.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but I keep coming back to this feeling that maybe I'm just not strong enough to handle loss the way other people do. Like, my aunt lost her too, and she's not falling apart, so what does that say about me? I guess I just worry that if I let myself fully feel this, it means I'm weak, or that I'm making it about me somehow.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — softly, carefully, like you're trying to take up as little space as possible — feels very connected to what you're actually saying, this fear that fully feeling your grief somehow makes you a burden or a problem. But I want to challenge that thought directly: strength isn't measured by how quickly you stop feeling, and your aunt's outward composure tells you nothing about her inner experience — it only tells you how she's *presenting*. Allowing yourself to grieve someone you loved deeply isn't making it about you; it *is* about you, and that's not only okay — it's necessary.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but there's this other voice that keeps saying if I really let myself fall apart over losing my dad, I'm just going to make everything harder for everyone else who's also grieving. Like, my aunt has been so composed through all of this, and I keep thinking maybe she's managing it better because she's stronger, or because she loved him differently than I did. And then I feel guilty for even thinking that, like I'm turning his death into some kind of competition about who's hurting more.
therapist: I notice you shifted from talking about your grandmother to your dad just now, and I want to gently hold space for that — it sounds like there may be even more loss here than we've touched on, and your words are coming very quickly, almost like you're trying to outrun the weight of it all. That thought that your grief is somehow a burden on others, or that your aunt's composure means she loved him "better" — that's a really painful story to be carrying, and it's worth noticing that it conveniently positions *you* as the problem rather than simply someone who is hurting. Grief isn't a competition, and shrinking your own pain to protect others from discomfort isn't strength — it's a way of abandoning yourself at the moment you need the most care.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're right, but it's not that simple. When I see my aunt just... holding it together at the funeral, greeting people, being so composed, it genuinely makes me feel like maybe I'm doing grief wrong, like there's something defective about how much I'm falling apart. And the idea that I'm "abandoning myself" sounds nice in theory, but honestly, making myself smaller has always been how I get through things without making everything worse for everyone else.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — very fast, pitched high, like something in you is wound tight and trying to hold it all together even as you describe falling apart — feels like a live demonstration of exactly what you're describing, this lifelong habit of managing yourself carefully so others don't have to feel the impact of your pain. I want to sit with what you just said: that making yourself smaller has "always" been how you get through things — because that's not a coping strategy you invented for this grief, that's something much older and deeper, and it deserves real attention. The fact that it's worked in the past doesn't mean it isn't costing you something significant right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hate that you noticed that, and I also kind of needed someone to notice that. It's like I've been performing "handling it okay" for so long that I didn't even realize I was doing it just now, in here, with you. And yeah, you're right that it's old — I think I learned pretty early that my feelings were kind of a burden to the people around me, so I just... got good at tucking them away.
therapist: What you just did — catching yourself performing "okay" in real time, in a safe space — is actually a profound moment, and I don't want it to slip by unnoticed. There's something in your voice right now that strikes me: you're speaking so softly, almost carefully, even as you're saying something enormous — that you learned as a child that your feelings were too much for the people who were supposed to hold them. That's not a small thing to carry, and it makes complete sense that grief, which demands to be felt, would be especially hard for someone who became an expert at making themselves invisible.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I didn't expect that to hit me so hard, but something about the way you said "making themselves invisible" just... I don't know, I felt my throat tighten. Because that's exactly it, isn't it — I didn't disappear because I wanted to, I disappeared because it felt like the only way to keep the peace, to keep people around me okay. And now my dad is gone and I don't even know how to grieve him properly because I'm still doing it, still shrinking, even here with you.
therapist: The tightening in your throat right now is your body recognizing something true — and I want you to hear this clearly: you didn't disappear because something was wrong with you, you disappeared because a child did what they had to do to feel safe and loved. And the fact that you can see yourself doing it *right now*, even here, even while your voice is moving so fast and your whole system feels wound up — that's not failure, that's the very beginning of something different, because you can't change a pattern you can't see. Your dad deserved to be grieved by the full version of you, and so do you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but there's this other part that keeps thinking... if I really did what I had to do to survive, then why does it still feel like a betrayal? Like I should have been stronger, or more present for him, especially at the end. And honestly, even sitting here right now, I can feel myself starting to speed up again, like if I just talk fast enough I can get through this without actually feeling it.
therapist: You just caught yourself in real time — speeding up, bracing, trying to outrun the feeling — and then you *stopped* and named it out loud, and that took real courage. I want to gently stay with the word "betrayal," because that thought — that surviving your own childhood somehow made you a worse son at the end of his life — is one of the cruellest things grief can whisper, and it deserves to be examined rather than outrun. You were doing the only thing you knew how to do, then and now, and learning a different way forward isn't a betrayal of him — it might actually be the most honest tribute you could offer.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but there's this stubborn voice that keeps pushing back. Like, if learning to cope better is a tribute to him, then why does it feel like I'm finally getting comfortable in a life he never got to finish living? I don't know, maybe that's the grief talking, but it feels like the more okay I become, the further away he gets.
therapist: What you just named — that fear that healing means losing him — is one of the most universal and least-talked-about parts of grief, and your voice right now, soft and careful and measured, sounds like someone holding something very fragile. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: getting more okay doesn't create distance from him, it just changes the *form* of his presence — he moves from being the shape of an open wound to being something you carry differently, something woven into who you're becoming. The goal was never to get so okay that he disappears; it's to find a way to keep him with you that doesn't require you to keep hurting.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
